It was the nineteenth round of the 2026 Formula One World Championship. Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari) took his first pole position since the 2023 Hungarian Grand Prix, and his first pole position with the team. Kimi Antonelli clinched his first Formula One World Drivers' Championship after achieving third. Antonelli became the youngest Drivers' Champion at the age of 20 years, two months and seven days, beating the previous record holder Sebastian Vettel, the first Italian Drivers' Champion since Alberto Ascari in 1953, and Mercedes' first Drivers' Championship since Hamilton secured his seventh title in 2020. Ahead of him, Max Verstappen (Red Bull) won the race and Hamilton finished second in an eventful race. The Grand Prix also saw Ryo Hirakawa make his Formula One Grand Prix debut with Haas, where he benefitted from drivers ahead of him receiving penalties to score his first Formula One point. == Background == The event was held at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez in Mexico City for the 26th time in the circuit's history, across the weekend of 30 October – 1 November, having previously held twenty editions of the Mexican Grand Prix. tool.excerpt: The 2026 Mexico City Grand Prix (officially known as the Formula 1 Gran Premio de la Ciudad de México 2026) was a Formula One motor race that was held on 1 November 2026 at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez in Mexico City, Mexico. It was the nineteenth round of the 2026 Formula One World Championship. Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari) took his first pole position since the 2023 Hungarian Grand Prix, and his first pole position with the team. Kimi Antonelli clinched his first Formula One World Drivers' Championship after achieving third. Antonelli became the youngest Drivers' Champion at the age of 20 years, two months and seven days, beating the previous record holder Sebastian Vettel, the first Italian Drivers' Champion since Alberto Ascari in 1953, and Mercedes' first Drivers' Championship since Hamilton secured his seventh title in 2020. Ahead of him, Max Verstappen (Red Bull) won the race and Hamilton finished second in an eventful race. The Grand Prix also saw Ryo Hirakawa make his Formula One Grand Prix debut with Haas, where he benefitted from drivers ahead of him receiving penalties to score his first Formula One point. == Background == The event was held at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez in Mexico City for the 26th time in the circuit's history, across the weekend of 30 October – 1 November, having previously held twenty editions of the Mexican Grand Prix. The Grand Prix was the ninteenth round of the 2026 Formula One World Championship and the sixth held under the name of the Mexico City Grand Prix, having previously been titled the Mexican Grand Prix. === Championship standings before the race === Going into the weekend, Kimi Antonelli led the Drivers' Championship with 365 points, 123 points ahead of teammate George Russell in second and 124 ahead of Lewis Hamilton in third. Mercedes, with 607 points, led the Constructors' Championship from Ferrari, who were second with 474 points, and Red Bull and McLaren, who both tied on 355 points. ==== Championship permutations ==== Going into the race, there were 125 points available across the five remaining scheduled rounds. Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari) took his first pole position since the 2023 Hungarian Grand Prix, and his first pole position with the team. Kimi Antonelli clinched his first Formula One World Drivers' Championship after achieving third. Antonelli became the youngest Drivers' Champion at the age of 20 years, two months and seven days, beating the previous record holder Sebastian Vettel, the first Italian Drivers' Champion since Alberto Ascari in 1953, and Mercedes' first Drivers' Championship since Hamilton secured his seventh title in 2020. Ahead of him, Max Verstappen (Red Bull) won the race and Hamilton finished second in an eventful race. The Grand Prix also saw Ryo Hirakawa make his Formula One Grand Prix debut with Haas, where he benefitted from drivers ahead of him receiving penalties to score his first Formula One point. == Background == The event was held at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez in Mexico City for the 26th time in the circuit's history, across the weekend of 30 October – 1 November, having previously held twenty editions of the Mexican Grand Prix. It was the nineteenth round of the 2026 Formula One World Championship. Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari) took his first pole position since the 2023 Hungarian Grand Prix, and his first pole position with the team. Kimi Antonelli clinched his first Formula One World Drivers' Championship after achieving third. Antonelli became the youngest Drivers' Champion at the age of 20 years, two months and seven days, beating the previous record holder Sebastian Vettel, the first Italian Drivers' Champion since Alberto Ascari in 1953, and Mercedes' first Drivers' Championship since Hamilton secured his seventh title in 2020. Ahead of him, Max Verstappen (Red Bull) won the race and Hamilton finished second in an eventful race. The Grand Prix also saw Ryo Hirakawa make his Formula One Grand Prix debut with Haas, where he benefitted from drivers ahead of him receiving penalties to score his first Formula One point. == Background == The event was held at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez in Mexico City for the 26th time in the circuit's history, across the weekend of 30 October – 1 November, having previously held twenty editions of the Mexican Grand Prix. The violence comes after the Group of Seven (G7) sounded the alarm on Wednesday over the “recent escalation of violence” in Sudan’s war, which erupted more than two and a half years ago. The war between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has killed tens of thousands of people, displaced nearly 12 million more and triggered one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. The violence has escalated dramatically in recent weeks, with the RSF seizing control of the key town of El-Fasher and with reports of atrocities multiplying. On Thursday, drones “targeted the army headquarters, the airport and the Merowe Dam,” an army statement said, adding that it had intercepted the attacks that it blamed on the RSF. Merowe is in an area that has been under army control for months. The town, about 330 kilometers (200 miles) north of the capital Khartoum, was plunged into darkness after a full power cut, witnesses told AFP . The RSF has increasingly resorted to drones in recent months, though the military also uses drones to conduct strikes. | Image: DRDO New Delhi, India - The Indian Army is ramping up its efforts to tackle the rising drone threat from across the Pakistan border with the acquisition of nine more laser-based anti-drone systems.

These Integrated Drone Detection and Interdiction Systems, developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation ( DRDO ), are proving crucial in curbing the growing use of drones for surveillance, smuggling weapons, and narcotics across the Line of Control (LoC) and the International Border (IB).

These laser-based anti-drone systems are already showing results.
India’s Counter-Drone Arsenal Set to Expand Further In addition to these 2-kilowatt laser-based systems, India is also working on a more advanced 30-kilowatt version.

Expected to be ready for deployment within two years, this advanced counter-drone tech is expected to raise India’s anti-aircraft capabilities to a whole new level, reinforcing the nation’s defence against aerial threats.

While the 2-kilowatt systems are currently operational, the upcoming 30-kilowatt systems will likely become a game-changer, offering expanded operational ranges and a more powerful response to large-scale drone threats.
With further advancements in counter-drone technology, India is positioning itself as a leader in this space.

tool.title: Rapid Support Forces
tool.excerpt: The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) are a Sudanese paramilitary force formerly operated by the Sudanese government. They originated as auxiliary force militias known as the Janjaweed used by the Sudanese government during the War in Darfur, which the government later restructured as a paramilitary organization in August 2013 under the command of Muhammad Dagalo, better known by his nom de guerre Hemedti. Since 2023, the RSF has been fighting a civil war against the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) for control of Sudan, after seizing power along with the SAF in the 2021 Sudanese coup d'état. In 2025, it established a parallel government called the Government of Peace and Unity in alliance with the Sudan People's Liberation Movement–North (SPLM–N). Its forces have been documented committing war crimes on a vast scale against members of non-Arab ethnicities in Darfur and against northern Sudanese Arabs (Ja'alin and Shaigiya) in Khartoum State and Gezira State because of their perceived support for the SAF. The United Arab Emirates has been widely accused of [withheld]ly supplying it with financial support. The RSF has obtained many fighters and arms from neighbouring Chad, the government of which has ceased any formal relations with Sudan in an effort to quell these accusations. RSF supply lines run in part through Libya, and RSF forces have been deployed to Libya to work for the Libyan National Army. Their fighters are largely recruited as mercenaries, with funding coming from the capture of gold mines and patronage by corporate and state actors; the group has also hired out its fighters as mercenaries to fight in conflicts and assist governments outside Sudan, such as in the Yemeni civil war (2014–present). In more recent years, the RSF has allegedly recruited mercenaries from more distant regions like Colombia to fight in its war in Sudan, occasionally via American-sanctioned firms in the United Kingdom. These Integrated Drone Detection and Interdiction Systems, developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation ( DRDO ), are proving crucial in curbing the growing use of drones for surveillance, smuggling weapons, and narcotics across the Line of Control (LoC) and the International Border (IB).

India’s Counter-Drone Arsenal Set to Expand Further In addition to these 2-kilowatt laser-based systems, India is also working on a more advanced 30-kilowatt version.

While the 2-kilowatt systems are currently operational, the upcoming 30-kilowatt systems will likely become a game-changer, offering expanded operational ranges and a more powerful response to large-scale drone threats.

tool.title: Rapid Support Forces
tool.excerpt: The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) are a Sudanese paramilitary force formerly operated by the Sudanese government. They originated as auxiliary force militias known as the Janjaweed used by the Sudanese government during the War in Darfur, which the government later restructured as a paramilitary organization in August 2013 under the command of Muhammad Dagalo, better known by his nom de guerre Hemedti. Since 2023, the RSF has been fighting a civil war against the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) for control of Sudan, after seizing power along with the SAF in the 2021 Sudanese coup d'état. In 2025, it established a parallel government called the Government of Peace and Unity in alliance with the Sudan People's Liberation Movement–North (SPLM–N). Its forces have been documented committing war crimes on a vast scale against members of non-Arab ethnicities in Darfur and against northern Sudanese Arabs (Ja'alin and Shaigiya) in Khartoum State and Gezira State because of their perceived support for the SAF. The United Arab Emirates has been widely accused of [withheld]ly supplying it with financial support. The RSF has obtained many fighters and arms from neighbouring Chad, the government of which has ceased any formal relations with Sudan in an effort to quell these accusations. RSF supply lines run in part through Libya, and RSF forces have been deployed to Libya to work for the Libyan National Army. Their fighters are largely recruited as mercenaries, with funding coming from the capture of gold mines and patronage by corporate and state actors; the group has also hired out its fighters as mercenaries to fight in conflicts and assist governments outside Sudan, such as in the Yemeni civil war (2014–present). In more recent years, the RSF has allegedly recruited mercenaries from more distant regions like Colombia to fight in its war in Sudan, occasionally via American-sanctioned firms in the United Kingdom. The report, “Intimidation and Persecution: Sudan’s Attacks on Peaceful Protesters and Physicians,” provides specific examples from December 19, 2018 through March 17, 2019 of targeted attacks on peaceful protests and medical professionals who support or treat protesters.

The report calls for accountability for members of the Sudanese government and security forces who have perpetrated crimes against protesters and the medical community and demands justice for the victims.

“The lethal attacks committed by the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan today are evidence that the violence against peaceful protesters in Sudan is once again on the rise,” said Maryam Al-Khawaja , European director and interim director of advocacy at Physicians for Human Rights .

In April, PHR released a report on massive violations of human rights committed by now-ousted Sudanese president Omar al-Bashir’s forces during the months of protests, including the use of disproportionate, unnecessary, and sometimes lethal force.
Physicians for Human Rights (PHR) has been tracking government violence against the Sudanese people since a round of protests began in December.

In subsequent weeks, doctors and other prisoners were released, the president was forced out of office and jailed, and dialogue ensued between leaders of opposition movements and newly appointed officials in a transitional council, most of whom were leaders in the previous government.

Since 2023, the RSF has been fighting a civil war against the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) for control of Sudan, after seizing power along with the SAF in the 2021 Sudanese coup d'état. In 2025, it established a parallel government called the Government of Peace and Unity in alliance with the Sudan People's Liberation Movement–North (SPLM–N). Its forces have been documented committing war crimes on a vast scale against members of non-Arab ethnicities in Darfur and against northern Sudanese Arabs (Ja'alin and Shaigiya) in Khartoum State and Gezira State because of their perceived support for the SAF. The United Arab Emirates has been widely accused of [withheld]ly supplying it with financial support. The RSF has obtained many fighters and arms from neighbouring Chad, the government of which has ceased any formal relations with Sudan in an effort to quell these accusations. RSF supply lines run in part through Libya, and RSF forces have been deployed to Libya to work for the Libyan National Army. While the 2-kilowatt systems are currently operational, the upcoming 30-kilowatt systems will likely become a game-changer, offering expanded operational ranges and a more powerful response to large-scale drone threats.

tool.title: Rapid Support Forces
tool.excerpt: The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) are a Sudanese paramilitary force formerly operated by the Sudanese government. They originated as auxiliary force militias known as the Janjaweed used by the Sudanese government during the War in Darfur, which the government later restructured as a paramilitary organization in August 2013 under the command of Muhammad Dagalo, better known by his nom de guerre Hemedti. Since 2023, the RSF has been fighting a civil war against the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) for control of Sudan, after seizing power along with the SAF in the 2021 Sudanese coup d'état. In 2025, it established a parallel government called the Government of Peace and Unity in alliance with the Sudan People's Liberation Movement–North (SPLM–N). Its forces have been documented committing war crimes on a vast scale against members of non-Arab ethnicities in Darfur and against northern Sudanese Arabs (Ja'alin and Shaigiya) in Khartoum State and Gezira State because of their perceived support for the SAF. The United Arab Emirates has been widely accused of [withheld]ly supplying it with financial support. The RSF has obtained many fighters and arms from neighbouring Chad, the government of which has ceased any formal relations with Sudan in an effort to quell these accusations. Yuvraj Tyagi Defence News 3 min read Follow : Laser-based anti-drone system.

| Image: DRDO New Delhi, India - The Indian Army is ramping up its efforts to tackle the rising drone threat from across the Pakistan border with the acquisition of nine more laser-based anti-drone systems.

These Integrated Drone Detection and Interdiction Systems, developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation ( DRDO ), are proving crucial in curbing the growing use of drones for surveillance, smuggling weapons, and narcotics across the Line of Control (LoC) and the International Border (IB).

Counter-Drone Efforts Intensify Amid Increasing Drone Infiltration The new systems are being introduced as part of the Army’s broader counter-terror and counter-infiltration strategy, especially aimed at Jammu and Kashmir.
The addition of nine more systems comes as part of a Defence Ministry-approved emergency procurement, which officials say is aimed at strengthening the Army’s defences in the region.
These laser-based anti-drone systems are already showing results.
India’s Counter-Drone Arsenal Set to Expand Further In addition to these 2-kilowatt laser-based systems, India is also working on a more advanced 30-kilowatt version.

Expected to be ready for deployment within two years, this advanced counter-drone tech is expected to raise India’s anti-aircraft capabilities to a whole new level, reinforcing the nation’s defence against aerial threats.

While the 2-kilowatt systems are currently operational, the upcoming 30-kilowatt systems will likely become a game-changer, offering expanded operational ranges and a more powerful response to large-scale drone threats.
With further advancements in counter-drone technology, India is positioning itself as a leader in this space.

sentences: Recently, one of the DRDO-developed systems successfully brought down a Pakistani drone in the 16 Corps area, which falls under the Army’s responsibility in Jammu.
The drone, which was spotted flying from Pakistan’s side, was swiftly neutralised by Army Air Defence units deployed south of the Pir Panjal ranges in Jammu, officials said.
With rising drone threats globally, India’s expertise in this area is quickly becoming a benchmark for other countries, highlighting its growing role in global security innovation.
Yuvraj Tyagi Defence News 3 min read Follow : Laser-based anti-drone system.

| Image: DRDO New Delhi, India - The Indian Army is ramping up its efforts to tackle the rising drone threat from across the Pakistan border with the acquisition of nine more laser-based anti-drone systems.

These Integrated Drone Detection and Interdiction Systems, developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation ( DRDO ), are proving crucial in curbing the growing use of drones for surveillance, smuggling weapons, and narcotics across the Line of Control (LoC) and the International Border (IB).

Counter-Drone Efforts Intensify Amid Increasing Drone Infiltration The new systems are being introduced as part of the Army’s broader counter-terror and counter-infiltration strategy, especially aimed at Jammu and Kashmir.
The addition of nine more systems comes as part of a Defence Ministry-approved emergency procurement, which officials say is aimed at strengthening the Army’s defences in the region.
These laser-based anti-drone systems are already showing results.
India’s Counter-Drone Arsenal Set to Expand Further In addition to these 2-kilowatt laser-based systems, India is also working on a more advanced 30-kilowatt version.

Expected to be ready for deployment within two years, this advanced counter-drone tech is expected to raise India’s anti-aircraft capabilities to a whole new level, reinforcing the nation’s defence against aerial threats.

While the 2-kilowatt systems are currently operational, the upcoming 30-kilowatt systems will likely become a game-changer, offering expanded operational ranges and a more powerful response to large-scale drone threats.
With further advancements in counter-drone technology, India is positioning itself as a leader in this space.

The RSF began launching attacks on the airport and other strategic sites in Khartoum state on Tuesday, on the eve of the reopening of the facility, which has been closed for more than two years.

tool.title: Rapid Support Forces
tool.excerpt: The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) are a Sudanese paramilitary force formerly operated by the Sudanese government. They originated as auxiliary force militias known as the Janjaweed used by the Sudanese government during the War in Darfur, which the government later restructured as a paramilitary organization in August 2013 under the command of Muhammad Dagalo, better known by his nom de guerre Hemedti. Since 2023, the RSF has been fighting a civil war against the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) for control of Sudan, after seizing power along with the SAF in the 2021 Sudanese coup d'état. In 2025, it established a parallel government called the Government of Peace and Unity in alliance with the Sudan People's Liberation Movement–North (SPLM–N). Its forces have been documented committing war crimes on a vast scale against members of non-Arab ethnicities in Darfur and against northern Sudanese Arabs (Ja'alin and Shaigiya) in Khartoum State and Gezira State because of their perceived support for the SAF. The United Arab Emirates has been widely accused of [withheld]ly supplying it with financial support. The RSF has obtained many fighters and arms from neighbouring Chad, the government of which has ceased any formal relations with Sudan in an effort to quell these accusations. RSF supply lines run in part through Libya, and RSF forces have been deployed to Libya to work for the Libyan National Army. Their fighters are largely recruited as mercenaries, with funding coming from the capture of gold mines and patronage by corporate and state actors; the group has also hired out its fighters as mercenaries to fight in conflicts and assist governments outside Sudan, such as in the Yemeni civil war (2014–present). In more recent years, the RSF has allegedly recruited mercenaries from more distant regions like Colombia to fight in its war in Sudan, occasionally via American-sanctioned firms in the United Kingdom. These Integrated Drone Detection and Interdiction Systems, developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation ( DRDO ), are proving crucial in curbing the growing use of drones for surveillance, smuggling weapons, and narcotics across the Line of Control (LoC) and the International Border (IB).

Expected to be ready for deployment within two years, this advanced counter-drone tech is expected to raise India’s anti-aircraft capabilities to a whole new level, reinforcing the nation’s defence against aerial threats.

While the 2-kilowatt systems are currently operational, the upcoming 30-kilowatt systems will likely become a game-changer, offering expanded operational ranges and a more powerful response to large-scale drone threats.

tool.title: Rapid Support Forces
tool.excerpt: The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) are a Sudanese paramilitary force formerly operated by the Sudanese government. They originated as auxiliary force militias known as the Janjaweed used by the Sudanese government during the War in Darfur, which the government later restructured as a paramilitary organization in August 2013 under the command of Muhammad Dagalo, better known by his nom de guerre Hemedti. Since 2023, the RSF has been fighting a civil war against the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) for control of Sudan, after seizing power along with the SAF in the 2021 Sudanese coup d'état. In 2025, it established a parallel government called the Government of Peace and Unity in alliance with the Sudan People's Liberation Movement–North (SPLM–N). Its forces have been documented committing war crimes on a vast scale against members of non-Arab ethnicities in Darfur and against northern Sudanese Arabs (Ja'alin and Shaigiya) in Khartoum State and Gezira State because of their perceived support for the SAF. The United Arab Emirates has been widely accused of [withheld]ly supplying it with financial support. The RSF has obtained many fighters and arms from neighbouring Chad, the government of which has ceased any formal relations with Sudan in an effort to quell these accusations. RSF supply lines run in part through Libya, and RSF forces have been deployed to Libya to work for the Libyan National Army. Their fighters are largely recruited as mercenaries, with funding coming from the capture of gold mines and patronage by corporate and state actors; the group has also hired out its fighters as mercenaries to fight in conflicts and assist governments outside Sudan, such as in the Yemeni civil war (2014–present). In more recent years, the RSF has allegedly recruited mercenaries from more distant regions like Colombia to fight in its war in Sudan, occasionally via American-sanctioned firms in the United Kingdom. tool.excerpt: With drones, many of them of Chinese origin, increasingly being used to carry out surveillance and illegal activities, India’s military is under pressure to find more efficient ways to deal with these small, but dangerous, aerial threats. The addition of nine more systems comes as part of a Defence Ministry-approved emergency procurement, which officials say is aimed at strengthening the Army’s defences in the region. These laser-based anti-drone systems are already showing results. Recently, one of the DRDO-developed systems successfully brought down a Pakistani drone in the 16 Corps area, which falls under the Army’s responsibility in Jammu. The drone, which was spotted flying from Pakistan’s side, was swiftly neutralised by Army Air Defence units deployed south of the Pir Panjal ranges in Jammu, officials said. ... sentences: Recently, one of the DRDO-developed systems successfully brought down a Pakistani drone in the 16 Corps area, which falls under the Army’s responsibility in Jammu.
The drone, which was spotted flying from Pakistan’s side, was swiftly neutralised by Army Air Defence units deployed south of the Pir Panjal ranges in Jammu, officials said.
With rising drone threats globally, India’s expertise in this area is quickly becoming a benchmark for other countries, highlighting its growing role in global security innovation.
Yuvraj Tyagi Defence News 3 min read Follow : Laser-based anti-drone system.

| Image: DRDO New Delhi, India - The Indian Army is ramping up its efforts to tackle the rising drone threat from across the Pakistan border with the acquisition of nine more laser-based anti-drone systems.

These Integrated Drone Detection and Interdiction Systems, developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation ( DRDO ), are proving crucial in curbing the growing use of drones for surveillance, smuggling weapons, and narcotics across the Line of Control (LoC) and the International Border (IB).

Counter-Drone Efforts Intensify Amid Increasing Drone Infiltration The new systems are being introduced as part of the Army’s broader counter-terror and counter-infiltration strategy, especially aimed at Jammu and Kashmir.
The addition of nine more systems comes as part of a Defence Ministry-approved emergency procurement, which officials say is aimed at strengthening the Army’s defences in the region.
These laser-based anti-drone systems are already showing results.
India’s Counter-Drone Arsenal Set to Expand Further In addition to these 2-kilowatt laser-based systems, India is also working on a more advanced 30-kilowatt version.

Expected to be ready for deployment within two years, this advanced counter-drone tech is expected to raise India’s anti-aircraft capabilities to a whole new level, reinforcing the nation’s defence against aerial threats.

While the 2-kilowatt systems are currently operational, the upcoming 30-kilowatt systems will likely become a game-changer, offering expanded operational ranges and a more powerful response to large-scale drone threats.
With further advancements in counter-drone technology, India is positioning itself as a leader in this space.

tool.title: Rapid Support Forces
tool.excerpt: The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) are a Sudanese paramilitary force formerly operated by the Sudanese government. They originated as auxiliary force militias known as the Janjaweed used by the Sudanese government during the War in Darfur, which the government later restructured as a paramilitary organization in August 2013 under the command of Muhammad Dagalo, better known by his nom de guerre Hemedti. Since 2023, the RSF has been fighting a civil war against the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) for control of Sudan, after seizing power along with the SAF in the 2021 Sudanese coup d'état. In 2025, it established a parallel government called the Government of Peace and Unity in alliance with the Sudan People's Liberation Movement–North (SPLM–N). Its forces have been documented committing war crimes on a vast scale against members of non-Arab ethnicities in Darfur and against northern Sudanese Arabs (Ja'alin and Shaigiya) in Khartoum State and Gezira State because of their perceived support for the SAF. The United Arab Emirates has been widely accused of [withheld]ly supplying it with financial support. The RSF has obtained many fighters and arms from neighbouring Chad, the government of which has ceased any formal relations with Sudan in an effort to quell these accusations. RSF supply lines run in part through Libya, and RSF forces have been deployed to Libya to work for the Libyan National Army. Their fighters are largely recruited as mercenaries, with funding coming from the capture of gold mines and patronage by corporate and state actors; the group has also hired out its fighters as mercenaries to fight in conflicts and assist governments outside Sudan, such as in the Yemeni civil war (2014–present). In more recent years, the RSF has allegedly recruited mercenaries from more distant regions like Colombia to fight in its war in Sudan, occasionally via American-sanctioned firms in the United Kingdom. tool.title: 2026 Bangladesh garment workers protests
tool.excerpt: The 2026 Bangladesh garment workers protests are a series of labour demonstrations by workers in the ready-made garment industry of Bangladesh, demanding an increase in the sector's minimum monthly wage from ৳12,500 to ৳30,000. Protests began in August 2026 and escalated in late October and early November 2026 in the industrial areas of Ashulia and Gazipur and in the capital, Dhaka. On 1 November 2026, the government announced the formation of a six-member Minimum Wage Board including factory owners, though protests continued after the announcement due to not meeting demands. == Background == Bangladesh's garment industry is the second-largest in the world, after China, and contributes about 10 percent of the country's gross domestic product. According to the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), the industry has around 4,000 registered factories employing more than four million workers, an estimated 65 percent of whom are women. The sector's previous minimum wage of ৳8,000 was in place from 2018 and, according to the Fair Labor Association, had fallen below the World Bank poverty line for a two- to three-person household by 2022. The association also found that garment workers' wages had barely increased since 2019 despite high inflation. The current minimum of ৳12,500 was declared by the Minimum Wage Board in November 2023. The decision was followed by protests in Gazipur, and the Clean Clothes Campaign described the new rate as a "poverty wage". In April 2026 an amendment to the Bangladesh Labour Act reduced the minimum wage review cycle for the sector from five years to three. The Global Living Wage Coalition, using the Anker methodology, estimated the 2025 monthly living wage at ৳30,459 for Dhaka City and ৳25,166 for the satellite cities and districts surrounding Dhaka, where most of the country's garment industry is located. — AFP Listen to article 1x 1.2x 1.5x comments Join our Whatsapp Channel Garment workers in Bangladesh staged a fourth day of wage protests on Tuesday, with police firing tear gas to disperse demonstrators as unrest disrupted factory operations and transport links in the country’s vital export sector.

The unrest, which began on Saturday, has intensified despite the government’s move to form a six-member wage board to review pay in Bangladesh’s garment sector, the world’s second-largest apparel exporter after China.
“It is crucial that brands act immediately and speak out in support of workers’ demands,” said Anne Bienias, from the Clean Clothes Campaign industry advocacy group.
The wage dispute comes amid mounting pressure on workers from rising prices.

“We are assessing any potential impact on our overall production and supply chain.” The Swedish company added it wanted adequate compensation for garment workers and remained committed to improving wages and working conditions.

Clashes were reported across industrial belts around Dhaka, including Ashulia, Gazipur and the capital’s Mirpur area, as workers staged fresh demonstrations and attempted to block major highways.

Industry officials warn prolonged closures could delay shipments and damage Bangladesh’s reputation as a reliable sourcing hub as it competes with rivals such as Vietnam and India for global apparel orders.
Factory owners said they are contending with rising operating costs, uncertainty in energy markets linked to conflict in the Middle East, and softer demand in key export markets.
They warn that prolonged unrest could disrupt production schedules and jeopardise export orders, while workers continue to press for higher wages and better working conditions.

tool.excerpt: The 2026 Bangladesh garment workers protests are a series of labour demonstrations by workers in the ready-made garment industry of Bangladesh, demanding an increase in the sector's minimum monthly wage from ৳12,500 to ৳30,000. Protests began in August 2026 and escalated in late October and early November 2026 in the industrial areas of Ashulia and Gazipur and in the capital, Dhaka. On 1 November 2026, the government announced the formation of a six-member Minimum Wage Board including factory owners, though protests continued after the announcement due to not meeting demands. == Background == Bangladesh's garment industry is the second-largest in the world, after China, and contributes about 10 percent of the country's gross domestic product. According to the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), the industry has around 4,000 registered factories employing more than four million workers, an estimated 65 percent of whom are women. The sector's previous minimum wage of ৳8,000 was in place from 2018 and, according to the Fair Labor Association, had fallen below the World Bank poverty line for a two- to three-person household by 2022. The association also found that garment workers' wages had barely increased since 2019 despite high inflation. The current minimum of ৳12,500 was declared by the Minimum Wage Board in November 2023. The decision was followed by protests in Gazipur, and the Clean Clothes Campaign described the new rate as a "poverty wage". In April 2026 an amendment to the Bangladesh Labour Act reduced the minimum wage review cycle for the sector from five years to three. (Sudanese Ministry of Energy and Petroleum/Handout via Xinhua) KHARTOUM, May 5 (Xinhua) -- Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have recently intensified drone attacks on areas controlled by the Sudanese army, a development that military experts regard as a dangerous escalation in their ongoing conflict. For the second consecutive day, a swarm of drones, allegedly fired by the RSF, targeted vital facilities in Port Sudan, the capital of the eastern Red Sea State. Since May 2023, the port city has served as the country's interim capital, housing the government and diplomatic missions. "Drones struck the city's fuel depots early in the morning, causing powerful explosions, fires, and thick plumes of smoke," an eyewitness told Xinhua. Videos shared by activists showed civil defense teams attempting to contain the blaze and prevent it from spreading to other depots. No human casualties have been reported so far. When visiting the targeted site, Energy Minister Mohieddin Naeem Mohamed Saeed denounced the strike as "a terrorist act" intended to destroy the largest fuel depots in Red Sea State. The minister called these strikes the latest in a series of systematic attacks by the militia on public services and civilian infrastructure, directly affecting the lives of citizens. The incidents occurred one day after RSF drones targeted a military airbase, a cargo warehouse, and civilian facilities in Port Sudan, marking the first attack on the city since the armed conflict erupted in mid-April 2023. Also on Monday, a military source told Xinhua that the army's air defenses intercepted a swarm of drones targeting Kassala Airport, the capital of Kassala State in eastern Sudan. tool.excerpt: The 2026 Bangladesh garment workers protests are a series of labour demonstrations by workers in the ready-made garment industry of Bangladesh, demanding an increase in the sector's minimum monthly wage from ৳12,500 to ৳30,000. Protests began in August 2026 and escalated in late October and early November 2026 in the industrial areas of Ashulia and Gazipur and in the capital, Dhaka. On 1 November 2026, the government announced the formation of a six-member Minimum Wage Board including factory owners, though protests continued after the announcement due to not meeting demands. == Background == Bangladesh's garment industry is the second-largest in the world, after China, and contributes about 10 percent of the country's gross domestic product. According to the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), the industry has around 4,000 registered factories employing more than four million workers, an estimated 65 percent of whom are women. The sector's previous minimum wage of ৳8,000 was in place from 2018 and, according to the Fair Labor Association, had fallen below the World Bank poverty line for a two- to three-person household by 2022. The association also found that garment workers' wages had barely increased since 2019 despite high inflation. The current minimum of ৳12,500 was declared by the Minimum Wage Board in November 2023. The decision was followed by protests in Gazipur, and the Clean Clothes Campaign described the new rate as a "poverty wage". In April 2026 an amendment to the Bangladesh Labour Act reduced the minimum wage review cycle for the sector from five years to three. The Global Living Wage Coalition, using the Anker methodology, estimated the 2025 monthly living wage at ৳30,459 for Dhaka City and ৳25,166 for the satellite cities and districts surrounding Dhaka, where most of the country's garment industry is located. The Dhaka City estimate is based on a family of four with 1.58 full-time workers and a monthly cost of a basic but decent living of ৳48,022. == Protests == === August–October 2026 === In August 2026, garment workers in several parts of the country held protests demanding a minimum wage of around ৳30,000, c

— AFP Listen to article 1x 1.2x 1.5x comments Join our Whatsapp Channel Garment workers in Bangladesh staged a fourth day of wage protests on Tuesday, with police firing tear gas to disperse demonstrators as unrest disrupted factory operations and transport links in the country’s vital export sector.

The unrest, which began on Saturday, has intensified despite the government’s move to form a six-member wage board to review pay in Bangladesh’s garment sector, the world’s second-largest apparel exporter after China.
“It is crucial that brands act immediately and speak out in support of workers’ demands,” said Anne Bienias, from the Clean Clothes Campaign industry advocacy group.
The wage dispute comes amid mounting pressure on workers from rising prices.

“We are assessing any potential impact on our overall production and supply chain.” The Swedish company added it wanted adequate compensation for garment workers and remained committed to improving wages and working conditions.
The government formed the wage board on November 1 to review pay in the garment sector, but the move has yet to calm the protests.

The industry employs about 4 million workers, supplies global brands such as H&M, Zara and Gap, and accounts for more than 80 per cent of the country’s export earnings.
Clashes were reported across industrial belts around Dhaka, including Ashulia, Gazipur and the capital’s Mirpur area, as workers staged fresh demonstrations and attempted to block major highways.

Industry officials warn prolonged closures could delay shipments and damage Bangladesh’s reputation as a reliable sourcing hub as it competes with rivals such as Vietnam and India for global apparel orders.
Factory owners said they are contending with rising operating costs, uncertainty in energy markets linked to conflict in the Middle East, and softer demand in key export markets.
They warn that prolonged unrest could disrupt production schedules and jeopardise export orders, while workers continue to press for higher wages and better working conditions.

The protests, which continued for the third day on Monday, come amid a prolonged economic slowdown, and just ahead of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina's proclaimed return to Bangladesh from exile in India.

As workers take to the streets amid rising inflation and stagnant wages, the government has accused Sheikh Hasina 's Awami League and "several people from across the border" of instigating the violence.
It was under Hasina that the ready-made garment industry, the backbone of Bangladesh's economy, grew massively.
The sector employs around four million workers, accounts for 80% of Bangladesh's export earnings and contributes about 10% of its GDP, according to data cited by Reuters.
However, the ready-made garment sector is now facing major disruption, with hundreds of factories shutting down over the weekend and nearly a million workers affected.
The demand comes amid a prolonged economic slowdown in Bangladesh .
The slowdown has also affected workers in the garment sector.

A Daily Star report published on October 22 noted that many garment workers were having to put in 16-hour shifts to earn Tk 19,000 to Tk 20,000 a month, barely enough to cover their families' expenses.

Following an emergency meeting with cabinet ministers late on Sunday, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman directed authorities to protect workers' interests while ensuring uninterrupted production in the garment sector.
That is why the Prime Minister has instructed everyone to be vigilant so that production in the garment sector is not disrupted and instability is not created," he told BBC Bangla.

The allegations went further on Monday, when Tarique's political assistant, Rashed Khan, accused Jamaat-e-Islami and the National Citizen Party (NCP) of instigating the protests, while claiming that Awami League and Chhatra League activists had joined demonstrations posing as garment workers.

In any case, for Bangladesh, the immediate challenge is twofold: restoring production in an industry that is critical to its export economy, while addressing the wage and working conditions that have brought its workforce onto the streets.
The violent protests, demanding higher wages, have brought large parts of its vital manufacturing sector to a standstill.

Although some factories reopened on Monday, protests continued across Dhaka and other major garment hubs.
The violence intensified the following day in Dhaka's Mirpur, where workers blocked the Mirpur-10 intersection and clashed with police.
Protesters hurled bricks and stones at security personnel, who responded with tear gas, water cannons and baton charges, Prothom Alo and United News of Bangladesh reported.
In Gazipur, protesters torched a police box in Konabari , a garment-waste warehouse and a pickup van in Kaliakair.
In neighbouring Savar and Ashulia, factory premises were vandalised and a security booth at a garment factory in Hemayetpur was set on fire.
The Daily Star reported that police dispersed workers attempting to take to the streets in Mirpur, while Prothom Alo reported a fresh blockade of the Dhaka-Tangail Highway in Gazipur.
Ten platoons of the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) were deployed in the district.
The unrest has severely disrupted garment production.
A heavy police force and Border Guard Bangladesh have been deployed to restore order in the industrial areas.
At the heart of the protests is a demand for higher wages.

tool.title: 2026 Bangladesh garment workers protests
tool.excerpt: The 2026 Bangladesh garment workers protests are a series of labour demonstrations by workers in the ready-made garment industry of Bangladesh, demanding an increase in the sector's minimum monthly wage from ৳12,500 to ৳30,000. Protests began in August 2026 and escalated in late October and early November 2026 in the industrial areas of Ashulia and Gazipur and in the capital, Dhaka. On 1 November 2026, the government announced the formation of a six-member Minimum Wage Board including factory owners, though protests continued after the announcement due to not meeting demands. == Background == Bangladesh's garment industry is the second-largest in the world, after China, and contributes about 10 percent of the country's gross domestic product. According to the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), the industry has around 4,000 registered factories employing more than four million workers, an estimated 65 percent of whom are women. The sector's previous minimum wage of ৳8,000 was in place from 2018 and, according to the Fair Labor Association, had fallen below the World Bank poverty line for a two- to three-person household by 2022. The association also found that garment workers' wages had barely increased since 2019 despite high inflation. The current minimum of ৳12,500 was declared by the Minimum Wage Board in November 2023. The decision was followed by protests in Gazipur, and the Clean Clothes Campaign described the new rate as a "poverty wage". In April 2026 an amendment to the Bangladesh Labour Act reduced the minimum wage review cycle for the sector from five years to three. The Global Living Wage Coalition, using the Anker methodology, estimated the 2025 monthly living wage at ৳30,459 for Dhaka City and ৳25,166 for the satellite cities and districts surrounding Dhaka, where most of the country's garment industry is located. tool.excerpt: The 2026 Bangladesh garment workers protests are a series of labour demonstrations by workers in the ready-made garment industry of Bangladesh, demanding an increase in the sector's minimum monthly wage from ৳12,500 to ৳30,000. Protests began in August 2026 and escalated in late October and early November 2026 in the industrial areas of Ashulia and Gazipur and in the capital, Dhaka. On 1 November 2026, the government announced the formation of a six-member Minimum Wage Board including factory owners, though protests continued after the announcement due to not meeting demands. == Background == Bangladesh's garment industry is the second-largest in the world, after China, and contributes about 10 percent of the country's gross domestic product. According to the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), the industry has around 4,000 registered factories employing more than four million workers, an estimated 65 percent of whom are women. The sector's previous minimum wage of ৳8,000 was in place from 2018 and, according to the Fair Labor Association, had fallen below the World Bank poverty line for a two- to three-person household by 2022. The association also found that garment workers' wages had barely increased since 2019 despite high inflation. The current minimum of ৳12,500 was declared by the Minimum Wage Board in November 2023. The decision was followed by protests in Gazipur, and the Clean Clothes Campaign described the new rate as a "poverty wage". In April 2026 an amendment to the Bangladesh Labour Act reduced the minimum wage review cycle for the sector from five years to three. The Global Living Wage Coalition, using the Anker methodology, estimated the 2025 monthly living wage at ৳30,459 for Dhaka City and ৳25,166 for the satellite cities and districts surrounding Dhaka, where most of the country's garment industry is located.
